# Jean de Labadie

The front cover of this brown leather book binding features elegant decorative stamping and gold-leaf lettering. In the upper center, the name **Jean de Labadie** <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674) was a former Jesuit priest who became a famous French Protestant minister and founded the Pietist communal sect known as the Labadists.</note> is stamped in gold. 

Below the name, a central blind-stamped <term>blind-stamped: a decorative technique where a design is impressed into the leather without using gold leaf or ink, leaving a subtle, colorless indentation</term> ornament in a diamond shape features a circular, cross-like motif. The cover is framed by a decorative border consisting of thin parallel lines and ornamental corner-pieces with stylized floral and scrollwork designs. To the left, the spine is visible, showing several compartments separated by raised bands, each decorated with a small stamped motif.

# PREFACE.

It has already been several years since this <term>treatise<note>original: "Tractaet"; a formal written work dealing systematically with a specific subject.</note></term> first appeared in Dutch, but not in its current state; for the author has since revised it and improved and expanded it with many things that seemed to be lacking for its completion.

Although he has given it a new title or name, he nevertheless wished to retain the old one, since the one could serve to explain the other, and both coming together might provide a better understanding of what the content and the purpose of the treatise is.

Thus, both these titles show, when examined, that the intent is only to present what belongs to true Christianity, and to point out the way to become true Christians. Therefore it is called a *Short Summary of True Christianity*, and a *Collection of Christian Fundamental Principles*, which not only teaches how to know it, but through a godly and Christian...

<vocab>Treatise, Author, Christianity, Short Summary of True Christianity, Collection of Christian Fundamental Principles</vocab>

<summary>This preface introduces a revised and expanded edition of a Dutch religious treatise, explaining that the author combined two titles to more clearly define the work's goal of teaching the principles of "true Christianity."</summary>
<keywords>treatise, revision, Christian principles, religious education, Dutch history</keywords>

Merely knowing Christianity and speaking of its foundations does not make one a Christian, but is the same as being a Jew, or even a <term>Pharisee<note>In the New Testament, Pharisees are often portrayed as religious leaders who strictly followed the letter of the law but were criticized by Jesus for hypocrisy.</note></term>; of whom it is said that they possessed and taught the <term>Law<note>original: "Wet"; referring to the religious and moral laws found in the Hebrew Bible.</note></term>, but none of them followed it, and were therefore judged by that law. In the same way, and with even greater severity, shall the Christian be judged by the words of Christ.

To speak well and not to act is to be judged by one's own mouth, like the <term>evil servant<note>A reference to a parable in the Gospel where a servant is punished for failing to fulfill his master's expectations.</note></term> in the <term>Gospel<note>original: "Evangelium"; the record of Jesus' life and teaching.</note></term>. *To believe that there is a God and a Christ,* without anything more, is to be like <term>Satan<note>original: "den satan"</note></term>, who believes the same; and often it is even worse. For there are many who say they believe yet do not tremble, but Satan not only believes, he trembles as well.

One can say with truth, in these extremely corrupt times—not only of Jews and Heathens, but also of those called Christians—*that there is little faith and fear of God on earth,* and

their books, is very vividly depicted. This must be our hope and our comfort: but in the meantime, one must think of first becoming a child again, before one can be a grown man.

To be a Christian child is to be a great man, and a truly perfect man; not by nature or by reason, but through <term>Grace<note>original: "Genade"; in Christian theology, the unmerited favor and divine assistance given to humans for their regeneration or sanctification.</note></term> and through <term>Faith<note>original: "Geloove"</note></term>, which cause him to grow as much in stature and measure as they cause him to increase in childhood. For the more someone in Christianity is like a child, the greater and more perfect a man he is. This <term>Treatise<note>original: "Tractaet"; a formal written work on a specific subject.</note></term>, aiming to form the Christian, places him immediately in the cradle, nurtures him further, and does not leave him until after having made him a perfect man—that is, a good Christian.

For greater usefulness, it is divided into many small <term>Articles<note>original: "Articulen"; distinct sections or points of discussion.</note></term>, like so many proverbs and concise arguments, which are easily remembered due to their brevity. Just as they awaken the spirit and the understanding, they do not burden the <term>memory<note>original: "memorie"</note></term>, which remembers them as easily as it grasps them.

<meta>This page continues the preface, shifting focus from the structure of the "Articles" mentioned previously to their practical effect on the reader. It argues that true Christianity is not a matter of intellectual theory but a transformation of the heart and will through grace.</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

Their pleasantness <note>original: "smakelickheyt"; literally "tastiness" or "savory quality," implying something that appeals to the spiritual palate or soul's "taste."</note> causes them to enter in, and reflection on them presses them deeper and causes them to be tasted repeatedly, so that they may be observed and put to work with greater desire and zeal.

For to read or to know them is of little value, and to profess them without living them is not much more. The **Christian Religion** <term>Christian Religion</term> <note>original: "Christelicke Religie"; here referring to the lived practice of faith rather than just institutional membership.</note> does not consist in mere speculation <term>speculation</term> <note>original: "speculatie"; meaning abstract intellectual theorizing without practical application.</note>. It is well enough known that **Faith** belongs as much to the heart as to the understanding, and it not only leads the understanding captive, but also binds and bridles the will. And since the will is itself the most stubborn and least docile, it must be made submissive with greater force. To this end, **Love**—which powerfully contends with the will—is full of sweet attractiveness, and **Grace** is a conquering delight. Once the head and the heart are won, the hand gives of itself; and works demonstrate faith and love as their natural fruits.

They follow and flow like living waters from these two fountains, which are actually but one, since faith, according to the **Apostle** <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul, specifically Galatians 5:6: "...faith which worketh by love."</note>, works through love.

## CHAPTER I.

### Concerning the Christian Religion and profession in general.

I. <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E with floral patterns in a square frame.</image-desc> To be a Christian and to be named as such / contains much more than one thinks. II. ## CHAPTER IV.

### Of the hatred of the World; the contempt for its goods, honor, and pleasure; and the renunciation of its desires, as well as its foundations and maxims.

I. Anyone who is truly called / drawn / and anticipated <note>original: *voorgekomen*; a reference to "prevenient grace," the theological concept that God's grace reaches out to a person before they have even turned toward Him.</note> by God with grace / to follow and serve Him; must first and before all things leave the world / withdraw their heart from it / and even their body as much as is possible / and renounce all its desires / with its foundations and <term>maxims</term> <note>The underlying rules or principles of worldly conduct.</note>. <margin>Matthew 6:24.</margin> Thus Christ has said / and judged that one cannot serve two Masters, God and <term>Mammon</term> <note>A biblical term for wealth or material greed, often personified as a false god.</note>, and that one must necessarily hate the one in order to love the other. This judgment must be followed / and executed against oneself / it not being possible that one can serve and love them both at the same time.

## II. 
The virtue for which nature has the least taste is the denial of oneself: <term>denial<gloss>Dutch: *verloocheninge*. This refers to the spiritual practice of "self-naughting" or "self-abnegation," where the believer sets aside their own ego and desires to make room for God's will.</gloss></term> one's life, esteem, will, and inclinations. One readily commits and accustoms oneself to all other virtues, but very little to this one. And there are souls who pray, fast, and give alms, who do not know what it is to deny or to hate themselves.

<margin>Matthew 22:37</margin>
## III. 
He who loves anything, whatever it may be, outside of God, has his heart in it; and having his heart in it, he does not love God with his whole heart. It matters little whether it is bound with a hair or with a cable; it is bound, and thereby attached to everything. <note>The author uses the metaphor of a bird: whether held by a thin thread or a heavy rope, the bird is equally prevented from flying. In the same way, even a "small" worldly attachment prevents the soul's ascent.</note> One must break everything, one as much as the other, in order to be loose and free, and to be bound to God alone. He who commanded us to love God with all our heart and all our soul has left nothing over. God does not actually receive the payment of this debt if even one penny is missing from it. If the heart still hangs by only a hair, God wants that hair too, even more than all the rest to which the heart is not attached.

## V. 
To begin the Christian life without beginning to <term>die to oneself<gloss>Dutch: *af te sterven*. A central concept in early modern mysticism and asceticism referring to "mortification"—the spiritual process of putting to death the ego, selfish desires, and personal will to allow God to act through the person.</gloss></term> is to wander from the very start, and to stumble with the first step. And one must return that far [to the beginning], after one has walked for a long time and done nothing but stray. For the more one advances off the path, the more one goes astray, and has exhausted oneself in vain.

## VI. 
There is nothing more dangerous for someone who begins to walk in the ways of God than to want to follow oneself or one's own heart without any other guide. It is given to but very few to walk the right path alone here. LIX. True Christian Humility consists in knowing oneself and God well: in seeing and feeling that, of oneself, one is pure Nothingness and sin; pure weakness and impotence, and simple corruption and wickedness; entirely incapable of thinking, willing, saying, or doing anything good. It also consists in recognizing oneself as unworthy of all esteem and honor, all divine or human service, and all grace, virtue, and heavenly gifts. Furthermore, it consists in considering oneself worthy of—and willingly enduring—all dishonor and scorn, poverty and illness, abandonment by God and by men, and all manner of spiritual and temporal evils.

Romans 5:3, 4.

LX. He who is truly humble shall also be patient; for Patience <note>original: "Lijdsaemheyt"</note> is the very natural sister of Humility. The one enables the bearing of suffering, just as the other acknowledges that one deserves to suffer. True patience sets no boundaries, but makes one ready to undergo all poverty, sickness, contempt, anxiety, distress, pain, and sorrow.

### XXVI.
In the practice of good works, one must not always strive after the greatest ones or those that cause a great stir, or seek only to perform those that are glorious and illustrious in themselves, highly visible, and come before the ears of the whole world—which then opens its mouth in wonder, applause, and exaltation of those same acts.

<margin>Matthew 6</margin> <note>A reference to the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus warns: "Take care not to practice your righteousness before men to be seen by them."</note>
<term>Ambition</term> <note>original: "Eersucht"; literally "hunger for honor."</note> and pride will often move and incite one toward such deeds. A desire for fame and to make a name for oneself leads one to undertake them. And one often receives his reward in the doing of them: namely, the flattery, praise, and approval of men. But the more vanity there is in an act, the less <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "deugt"; moral excellence or strength.</note> it contains; and the more a person has sought and found themselves in the act, the less God is found therein.

### XXVII.
The best works, most pleasing to God and most abundant in steadfast virtue, are commonly those that have little outward appearance and do not cause a great stir before people. God, being the only one who sees and the secret witness thereof, views them with all the more pleasure. Also, in such humble, minor, and <term>simple</term> <note>original: "slechte"; in the 17th century, this meant "plain," "unassuming," or "lowly" rather than "bad."</note> works, there is indeed the greatest humility, <term>mortification</term>, <note>original: "doodinge"; the spiritual practice of "killing off" or subduing the selfish ego and worldly desires.</note> and overcoming of oneself, and a more pure love of God, for whom and before whose eyes alone these works are performed.

<summary>This page warns against performing "good works" for the sake of public recognition and pride, arguing that humble, quiet acts of service are more virtuous and pleasing to God.</summary>

XVII. **Jesus** kept Himself private and hidden for thirty years, only to live in public for three years. **John the Baptist** remained hidden and in obscurity even longer. The **Apostles** of the Lord were quiet and private for a long time. And generally, the greatest and holiest men of the **Church** kept themselves hidden and silent for a long time before they revealed themselves to the world and spoke. Their first inclination and disposition was toward solitude and the private life; they did not enter into public life except when compelled, and always after they had spent some time in a private life.

<page-num>290</page-num>
<header>Summary</header>

...as well to hold an office <note>The Dutch word "bedieninge" refers to both religious ministry and public office.</note> as to be idle and of no use to anyone; and to receive the honor of the office, provided it is accompanied by fruitfulness, as it is to enjoy the benefit of having no office at all. One is fit to be in an office when one is ready to be without that office; and he who accepts it, while being ready to lay it down, is fit to possess it and to serve in it properly.

XXII. One has need of Grace, and much grace, for a public life. One must have it for almost everything, because of the great variety of temperaments <note>Original: "gemoederen," referring to the diverse dispositions, moods, or characters of the people one must lead.</note> and matters that one must govern and handle. Grace must accompany the office, and must come from God no less than the office itself. Without grace, the office is but a burden and heavy servitude. A body without a soul is like an immovable block of wood: so is the office without the spirit and grace required for it, which one must consequently request from God. If one possesses these, then the service will be as if alive, light to bear, and able to be performed well. The service of a Teacher <term>Leeraer: in this context, a minister or doctrinal instructor</term> or Shepherd <note>Herder: a pastor or spiritual leader.</note> is of one kind, and that of an Authority <term>Overigheypt: the magistracy or civil government leaders</term> is another. They have need of diverse graces: just as the grace of a married person is different from the grace of an unmarried person, and that of a king is even more different from that of a subject.

<summary>This page concludes that a person is only fit for public or religious office if they are willing to give it up, and argues that such roles require specific divine grace to manage the complexities of human nature and governance.</summary>

# XV. CHAPTER.
## Of the Solitary and Retired Life.

I. Here we are not dealing with an outward, physical solitude, in which beasts and the wildest animals live; in which fools and the most deranged fools dwell; nor even that in which philosophers—and the most melancholy and peevish <note>original: "verdrietelickste," implying someone who is tiresome, irritable, or perpetually dissatisfied.</note> philosophers—reside; nor even that in which prisoners and great criminals often live and are placed: but of an inner, spiritual Solitude, which can exist without the physical kind, and is not bound to it. The other <note>referring to purely physical isolation</note> generally has something that tastes more or less of savagery, or also of violence and coercion, and therefore seldom possesses anything that corresponds with **Christian Solitude**; and not having that which is sufficiently according to the nature of men, how could it be according to the **Spirit of God**?

### VI.

A truly retired <note>original: "geretireert," meaning a life of spiritual withdrawal or seclusion from worldly affairs</note> life is no matter of small importance. To find a truly retired or rightly solitary person in these days is something rare. Many bear the name of it, who have nothing of the deed; and most who nowadays call themselves monks or solitaries are nothing but a name, and are [hardly] set apart <note>original: "afgesondert," a term for being consecrated or separated for holy use</note> before God. The clothing, the solemn face, or even the partition <note>original: "afschepisel," referring to a dividing wall or a cloistered cell</note> of thick walls, do not make a true or spiritual solitary and set-apart person. These things cannot set boundaries for the spirit as they do for the bodies. He who goes and comes so much in and among the world—and that in the vain, restless, curious, and lustful spirit of the world—is without doubt of the world, and very much so. Many seem for a time to leave the world through one door, who soon return through two others: and their return brings them deeper into it than their first entry into the world. For before they were in it as if by nature, and afterward they return to it [with intent].

### XIV. 
The world being an enemy of God, who exerts all her powers against Him, seeks nothing else than to lead away His chosen Flock. The <term>retired life: "geretireerde leven," a life of spiritual retreat or seclusion</term> is like a suitable Harbor where this wind does not blow, and like a good <term>roadstead: "Ree," a sheltered offshore anchorage</term>, beyond the reach of the turbulence of these waves. One must reach this Harbor if one wishes to escape the storm. Its sweetness and its peace are as useful as they are pleasant; and by being far from honor and greatness, it protects from the tempest and danger that <term>salvation: "saligheyt"</term> faces.

### XVII.
A truly penitent life—necessarily binding one to a proper abstinence from all unlawful, or even lawful, pleasures which one might misuse as they have been misused before—also necessarily binds one to a retired life, which draws one away from such things. Humility is not often found among the magnificent retinues of the Courts. It is not at feasts and costly meals that one mixes one’s bread with ashes and dips it in one’s tears. It is not in the midst of ballets and dances that one abandons oneself to much weeping, nor on the stage that one plays the role of a true penitent. ### XXI. 
It is beyond all doubt that a Christian owes great duties to God, such as those of worship and praise, of prayer and sacrifice, of heavenly conversation and holy union with Him. These are duties he must practice and with which he must also become intimately acquainted. Now, it is very difficult to worship often and in peace while living a worldly and vain life. How shall one worship God in spirit and in truth <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 4:24</note> when the senses wander toward all sorts of objects, and the whole person is encumbered with the vain things of this world? Worldly occupations fragment one's prayer and take away all of one's time. The bustle of the age <note>original: "omslag der eeuwe," referring to the distractions and spirit of the current worldly era</note> does not allow one to deal with God in peace. And the multitude of worldly social circles excludes His company and greatly disrupts one’s communion with Him. The <term>retired life: "geretireerde leven," a life of spiritual solitude and withdrawal from society</term> alone provides the time to worship God, to enter into an intimate communion and union with Him, and to become and remain as one heart and spirit with Him.

XXXVIII. This also shows that it is good / in whatever state of secluded and holy life one may be / not to bind oneself to something firmly or forever / not only to keep out all compulsion / but also to avoid, as it were, binding **God’s** hands / which must always remain free / and who at all times wishes to be able to do with **His** creature whatever **He** wills. One may add to this / that he is also not assured of always having that same heart or that same grace. For if the **Lord** ceases to want that thing from him any longer / then **He** will also undoubtedly cease giving him the spirit for it / without which man can do nothing, no matter what force <note>original: *gewelt*, meaning effort or spiritual striving</note> he might exert. And so he will be found to have promised / that which he will not be able to keep / and to have made for himself a bond that he will not easily be able to break; indeed, to have laid a bond upon **God** / which **His Spirit** will eventually break / which will cause much suffering to the soul / which / whatever path **God** pleases to take with it / must always remain in a state and ready to obey **Him** and to follow **Him** into another [path] / to which it must also no more bind itself than to the one it has just now left.

A completely solitary life <note>original: *eenſaem leven*, referring to the life of a hermit or recluse</note> is far too burdensome to be undertaken without a calling and grace that is somewhat extraordinary. He who does not have this, and does not have it at all times, runs great danger of becoming weary in it, being very idle, and losing his time, without gaining anything other than torment. If (as we have said, and cannot say enough) the soul is not properly occupied with God therein; if one does not love spiritual contemplation <term>spiritual contemplation: the practice of quiet, prayerful focus on divine truths</term> and the grace of prayer; if one does not have a great taste for the Scriptures, and pleasure even in physical labor, then one will very easily become either wild or melancholy <note>original: *ſwaermoedig*, a term often used in this period to describe a deep spiritual depression or "religious melancholy"</note>, and as unhealthy in body as in soul; for both are corrupted by such a forced life. A completely solitary state without an abundance of grace and great communion with God is a very sorrowful state in this life, which also opens the door to all kinds of temptations, distractions, and troubles, under which a heart easily fails and withers away. Such a life, then, is more capable of making one dull and animal-like than spiritual and heavenly.

### XXXVIII. This also shows that it is good—in whatever state of secluded <note>original: *geretireert*, meaning a life withdrawn from the world for religious reasons</note> and holy life one may be—not to bind oneself firmly or forever to it. This is not only to keep out all external compulsion, but also so as not to "bind the hands of God," as it were; for His hands must always remain free, as He wishes to be able to do with His creature <note>original: *schepsel*, referring to the human being as a created work of God</note> whatever He wills at all times. 

He who binds himself to that which is in itself indifferent <term>indifferent: refers to *adiaphora*, or actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God, and thus spiritually neutral</term> does not know whether God might later want the opposite <note>original: *contrary*</note> from him. To this one can add that he is also not certain of always possessing that same heart or that same grace. For if the Lord ceases to desire that particular way of life from him, He will undoubtedly also cease to give him the spirit for it—and without that spirit, a person can achieve nothing, no matter how much force they might exert. 

And so, such a person will be found to have promised what they cannot easily keep. They will have made a bond for themselves that they cannot easily break; indeed, they will have attempted to place a bond upon God, which His Spirit will ultimately shatter. This will bring great suffering to the soul, which—no matter what path God chooses to lead it upon—must always remain in a state of readiness to obey Him and follow Him into another way of life. Furthermore, the soul must not bind itself to this new path any more than it did to the one it is currently leaving.

<summary>The author argues against making permanent, rigid vows to a specific religious lifestyle, explaining that believers must remain flexible so that God can lead them to different paths as His grace dictates.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual freedom, vows, adiaphora, divine will, grace, seclusion, obedience, religious life</keywords>

### XXXIX. 

A completely solitary life <note>original: *eensam leven*</note> is far too difficult to be undertaken without a calling <term>calling: *roepinge*, the internal conviction that God has summoned a person to a specific way of life</term> and grace that is somewhat extraordinary. He who does not have this—and does not have it at all times—runs a great danger of becoming weary in it, of falling into idleness, and of losing his time, without gaining anything other than torment. 

If (as we have said, and cannot say enough) the soul therein is not properly occupied with God; if one does not love spiritual contemplation <note>original: *geestelicke beschouwinge*</note> and the grace of prayer; if one does not have a great taste for the Scriptures, and even pleasure in physical labor, then one will very easily become either wild or melancholy <note>original: *swaermoedig*, a term used historically to describe both spiritual depression and a physical imbalance of the humors</note>, and as unhealthy in body as in soul; for both are ruined by such a forced life. 

An entirely solitary state without an abundance of grace and great communion with God is a very sorrowful state in this life, which also opens the door to all kinds of temptations, distractions, and troubles, under which a heart easily faints and wastes away. Such a life then is more suited to making one dull and animal-like than spiritual and heavenly.

## CHAPTER XVI.

Regarding the Ways of God and of His Spirit over souls. Regarding the signs [to know] if one has received that Spirit, and is moved by Him, and led in the ways of God. And regarding the simplicity and faithfulness required to follow Him, especially in poverty, scorn, pain, and outward and inward suffering, in conformity with Jesus Christ.

I. <margin>Rom. 11: 33, 34.</margin> THE Ways of God are Divine <note>original: *Goddelick*</note>—that is—incomprehensible and unsearchable <note>original: *onnaspeurlick*; meaning they cannot be traced or fully tracked by human logic</note>. Thus the Scripture <term>Scripture: *Schriftuur*, the Bible</term> calls them, which also at once gives them the name of depths and abysses. But because they exceed the understanding and grasp of man, they are nonetheless no less rational and grounded. Being deep abysses <note>original: *afgronden*</note>, they are nevertheless full of the wisdom and the knowledge of God, who is greater than man, and whose mind no one has known. The mind of God often goes as much against as it goes above the mind of man. <margin>Isa. 55: 9.</margin> Just as the heaven is higher than the earth (says the Prophet <term>Prophet: *Propheet*, referring here to Isaiah</term>): so are His Ways higher than our ways, and His thoughts higher than our thoughts. He does not call us into His Counsel <term>Counsel: *Raet*, referring to God’s private deliberations or sovereign plans</term>. He is our sovereign Lord <note>original: *souvereynen Heere*</note> and the Lord of all, who does what He wills in heaven and on earth. Our understanding and senses

VIII. ### Summary

...unspeakable <note>The Dutch text "sprekelicke" completes the word "onuitsprekelicke" from the previous page, meaning "inexpressible" or "unspeakable."</note> Fundamental Rule: that one must want everything that God wants; that nothing is more just than that the creature be subject to the Creator in all things, and that He may do with it according to His good pleasure; that His pleasure must be ours, and all that is ours must be His alone. His will is our Rule, and the measure of good and evil; everything being good and very good as soon as He wills it. According to this will of His, the Patriarchs <term>Patriarchs: the early biblical fathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob</term>, the Prophets, the Apostles, and so many great Saints have regulated themselves, doing nothing else but following God and doing His will through faith and love.

XXXII. God has made their hearts spacious and their legs strong: otherwise the one [the heart] would not have been large enough to house Him, and the other [the legs] not firm and steady enough to avoid faltering in His ways, and to run in them readily. One only has to look at those whom He guided <margin>Hebrews 11</margin>—Abraham and Isaac, Joseph, and Moses, the other Prophets after them, the Apostles, the Martyrs, and many other Believers—to notice that one must not limit Him in anything, and that He does not limit Himself, nor does He always conform to our boundaries and weaknesses; but rather that He wants us to conform ourselves to Him and to His infinity, both in power and in will.

XXXIII. As long as we [remain] within our boundaries...

### of the most important subjects.

* Love consists in doing the same <note>Referring to the Will of God.</note>. 447.
* In everything, regard must be had for the same. 447.
* Out of love, one must readily unite oneself with the same in all things. 447. 448. 461-165. <note>The number 165 is likely a printer's error for 465.</note>
* Our own will spoils everything and must be completely denied. 448. 449.
* Embracing God's will in everything is the best way of dealing with God. 411.
* Willing submission to the same in all things is a sign of our <term>deadness to self<note>Dutch: *afgestorvenheyt*. A common spiritual term in the 17th century for "mortification," or the process of dying to one's own worldly desires to become more alive to God.</note></term>. 449.
* Nothing should occupy us in this life except only the will of God. 451. 453.
* By doing the same, we make God our ultimate End. 452.
* By using <term>creatures<note>Dutch: *schepselen*. This refers to all created things in the natural world, including people and objects, rather than just animals.</note></term> according to the same, we find God in them. 452.
* Through union with God's will, life and death are one and the same to the Believer. 454. 456.
* One reaches true tranquility and simplicity by seeing God and His will in everything. 456.
* The will of God is the great Rule of the Saints. 260.
* He who truly loves the same embraces everything God does, as much in His justice as His grace. 464. 465.
